newsitem.title: FRANCE: FOCUS-New Bank of France team leaves rates alone.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-New Bank of France team leaves rates alone.

text.p: A new Bank of France team held a key interest rate unchanged on Thursday in what some saw as a sign from the independent central bank it was sticking to its cautious policy despite the appointment of two new members.

The bank, whose nine-member monetary policy council held its first meeting since Pierre Guillen and Jean-Rene Bernard joined the policy-setting body this month, said it was leaving its intervention rate at 3.15 percent.

Economists said while the decision might have been meant to dampen speculation that the new members, seen as close to French President Jacques Chirac, would lead to faster rate cuts, the bank would probably still trim rates in coming months.

"I'd say it's a fairly cautious approach, in part designed to quash speculation the two new council members would instantly advocate looser monetary policy," Sonja Gibbs, bond strategist at Nomura International, said.
"It doesn't change expectations at all for rate cuts in the first quarter of at least 10 to 15 basis points," she said.

Expectations of rate cuts have been building since some Bank of France council members broke ranks last year and urged larger reductions, adding to calls from politicians for a more aggressive easing of policy to boost economic growth.

The two new members were seen as tipping the balance at the bank in favour of those who advocate faster cuts, resisted in the past by central bank governor Jean-Claude Trichet to avoid a weakening of the franc.

The bank has traditionally maintained a small premium over Germany's repo rate, now at 3.00 percent, to cushion the franc against attack on currency markets and defend its link to the mark, seen as the cornerstone of a European single currency.

Economists said a significant move after the first meeting of the new council could have left the independent bank open to accusations that its decisions were being influenced by politicians, keen to bring down record unemployment.

Some economists said, however, that even if the new members did have close ties to Chirac, his declaration in December that there was no question of abandoning the strong franc, or "franc fort", policy meant that no revolution was on the cards.
Chirac said then that a weakening of the franc against the mark "would be a rupture of the Franco-German partnership and then we would face a major European crisis".

Although the decision to leave rates steady was at odds with forecasts by private economists -- two thirds of those polled by Reuters expected a cut -- bond and interest rate futures emerged unscathed as the hope for cuts in due course provided support.
"It's slightly disappointing for the market. There were strong expectations built on a rate cut," Philippe Brossard, economist at ABN-Amro, said.
But he said he still believed the bank's council had turned more "dovish" -- softer on monetary policy -- and expected it to try to bring French official rates down to the level of Germany.

Economists said the Bank of France might well offer a hint of more intervention rate cuts to come by lowering the overnight rate, seen as a semi-official interest rate, before the next meeting on January 30.

"Sometime in the next two weeks...assuming the franc holds its current level, we could see at least a small gesture on (the overnight rate)," Patrick Mange, economist at Deutsche Bank in Paris, said. "The Bank of France's objective remains to bring French rates down to the level of German rates."

The franc was trading around 3.3750 per mark, slightly below 3.35, its central parity against the mark in the European Exchange Rate Mechanism (ERM) -- a level meant to reflect economic fundamentals in France and Germany.

Sean Shepley, international economist at CS First Boston, said another reason for the central bank's inaction might have been that it was waiting for more accurate data on the state of the economy in the last three months of 1996.
